narrative:
The model predicted an 82% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students. This signal of relative academic performance weighed heavily against your application.

Next, your LSAT score of 22.5 also pulled the prediction toward failure. It sits well below the average of 37 among those who were admitted, indicating the model saw this as another clear risk factor for bar exam success.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 worked in the opposite direction, modestly supporting a higher chance of passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to offset the two stronger negative influences.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of low class standing and a low LSAT score created too great a risk of first-time bar failure.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas within your control. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, strengthen your academic performance if you are still in school, and consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence of stronger readiness for the bar exam. Many students improve these metrics and gain admission on a later attempt.
